analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire Affordable Care Act and restores the law as it existed before.
analysis.headline: Introduced the day after the health law was signed, the repeal bill was sent to eight committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act in its entirety — the coverage expansion, Medicaid growth, insurance rules, and taxes — and put the old law back in place as if the ACA had never passed. It was introduced on March 24, 2010, the day after President Obama signed the ACA, with 28 Republican cosponsors. The House's Democratic majority referred it to eight committees, none of which ever held a hearing or markup, and it died without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be higher-income households and employers. The bill would repeal the ACA's Medicare-related taxes, including the additional 0.9% payroll tax on wages above $200,000 for singles ($250,000 for couples) and the 3.8% tax on most investment income for those same households, and it would end the employer mandate penalties. Large employers would no longer face assessments for not covering workers, and medical device makers would be relieved of the law's excise tax. People who opposed the individual mandate or the law's regulations would also be relieved of those requirements.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the ACA and restores every provision of law the ACA amended or repealed, so all of the law's taxes, mandates, and programs disappear retroactively to the ACA's enactment date.

Repealing the law ends the Medicare payroll surtax on high wages and the surtax on investment income that apply to households above roughly $200,000–$250,000, directly lowering taxes for high earners.
Repeal eliminates the employer responsibility penalties and the individual mandate, so large employers and people who did not want to buy insurance would owe nothing under those provisions.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the people who had just gained from the law would lose it: the uninsured who would have qualified for Medicaid expansion and subsidized private coverage, people with pre-existing conditions newly protected from being denied insurance, young adults allowed to stay on a parent's plan until age 26, and seniors and beneficiaries who benefited from the law's Medicare improvements. The federal government would also have to unwind the law's funding mechanisms without any replacement coverage in place.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would take away the ACA's core coverage protections with nothing replacing them — the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions, the Medicaid expansion, premium subsidies, the extension of dependent coverage to age 26, and the small-business and low-income tax credits all disappear.

The bill restores the pre-ACA insurance market, in which insurers could deny or cancel policies and charge sick people more, and leaves the tens of millions of people projected to gain coverage under the law back where they started.

Supporters of repeal acknowledged the law added costs and mandates; an honest objection in the other direction is that this bill offers no gradual unwind or replacement, only a clean erasure that would strand people and programs mid-transition — the ACA had been signed the day before the bill was introduced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real relief to specific groups — high earners paying the Medicare surtaxes, employers facing mandate penalties, and people opposed to the mandate — but it pays for that by stripping away the coverage expansions and insurance protections that had just become law, with no replacement of any kind. Because it was a full repeal of a brand-new statute, the costs to newly covered and newly protected households would have landed immediately, while the tax relief would go mostly to the top of the income scale. Weighed honestly, the benefits flow to concentrated interests while the costs fall broadly.

outcome.mechanism: The Democratic majority sent it to eight committees the day it was introduced; none of them ever held a hearing or markup, and it expired without a vote when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Connie Mack introduced the bill on March 24, 2010, the day after the ACA was signed into law, with 28 Republican cosponsors.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to eight committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Appropriations, and Rules — with two subcommittees later taking referrals.
No committee ever reported the bill, and the record shows no floor action of any kind before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

The House majority at the time was Democratic, 253 Democrats to 178 Republicans, and Democrats had just passed the ACA, so the majority had every procedural means to keep the bill from advancing — and did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households that had just gained ACA coverage and protections are better off because the bill never advanced, and so are health insurers whose subsidized new customers and mandate survived. For Republicans, the outcome carried little cost — the bill was a statement measure that never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households covered by the new health law

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — one sponsor and 28 of 178 House Republicans as cosponsors — while the Democratic majority of 253 kept the bill in committee and never scheduled any action on it.

industries.note: The ACA created the individual mandate and federal subsidies that steer millions of new paying customers through private insurers; full repeal would have removed that guaranteed market. Insurers' interest in keeping the law ran alongside ordinary people's interest in keeping coverage.
Repeal erases the ACA's Medicare payroll surtax on high wages and its 3.8% surtax on investment income, a direct tax cut that accrues almost entirely to households above roughly $200,000–$250,000.
Repeal ends the employer mandate penalties for not offering qualifying coverage, removing a cost employers would otherwise bear — and the coverage workers would have gained along with it.
The ACA imposed an excise tax on medical device sales; this bill would eliminate it, cutting the industry's tax bill.
